# Lights for the justice that Colombia needs for peace.

**Academics and lawyers, both national and international, met at EAFIT to discuss the justice system and the peace process.**

**The seminar featured the participation of prominent representatives from the International Criminal Court, the Max Planck Institute (Germany), judges from the Constitutional Court and the JEP, as well as professors from EAFIT and the Externado University of Colombia.**

- [Start](https://www.eafit.edu.co/)
- [News](https://www.eafit.edu.co/noticias)
- [Our Impact](https://www.eafit.edu.co/noticias/nuestro-impacto)
- Lights for the Justice That Colombia Needs for Peace

![Image: Lights for the justice that Colombia needs for peace](https://universidadeafit.widen.net/content/92cffe3e-4f24-4294-9b1e-80f2b1e3bfae/web/justicia-trnasicional1500.jpg?crop=yes&k=c&w=823&h=450&itok=KOjU9SzP)

The international recognition of the peace process in Colombia has attracted the attention of criminal law experts around the world, several of whom were invited to this forum held at EAFIT.

To safeguard the agreements and offer the legal security that the peace process requires. That, according to Judge José Fernando Reyes Cuartas, has been the vision of the Constitutional Court of Colombia regarding the transitional justice with which the country intends to overcome the armed conflict with the FARC.

The magistrate presented the balance of the work of that national legal entity in relation to the peace agreement before national and international experts convened at the seminar Transitional Justice: the Colombian model, which concludes this Friday, June 1st at EAFIT.

This meeting—organized by the EAFIT School of Law and Continuing Education, together with the Max Planck Institute for Foreign and International Criminal Law, and the Center for Research in Philosophy and Law of the Externado University of Colombia—made it clear that the Colombian case has become an international benchmark for the peace process and the implementation of a new justice model.

Judge Reyes Cuartas believes this interest stems from the fact that it may be a unique case in the world, among other reasons because “it is not a conflict between dictatorships, which is generally where studies on transitional justice have been developed. The Colombian process is authentic because, in the context of the International Criminal Court, which, for example, was not present in the Central American processes, new guidelines for progress in the concept of transitional justice are emerging.”

The national case is being addressed from various legal perspectives, and therefore the seminar discussed the relationship between international criminal justice and national criminal justice; the special justice system in Colombia and the Constitutional Court's proposals; the command responsibility of the various actors in the armed conflict; and the role of law in post-conflict societies.

###### Legal protection

Several international analysts who presented their studies during the meeting agreed that for the restoration of peace and security, not only is the transitional justice process fundamental, but also the legislative developments, as well as the constitutional validity that these have received through the various rulings of the Court, giving legal protection to the agreements for the next three periods of government.

Likewise, the seminar served as a platform to highlight key areas requiring attention. For example, German jurist Klaus Günther, a professor at the University of Frankfurt (Germany), stated that the relationship between international criminal justice and national criminal justice, from a legal perspective, is largely aligned. However, conflicts between these two systems generally arise when mandates based on national laws violate the international human rights of a group of individuals on a massive and sustained basis, as in the case of the armed conflict in Colombia.

“Indeed, one of the functions of international criminal law is to restore confidence in the validity of human rights. International criminal law constitutes the normative expectation of a citizen, in their dual role as a citizen of a nation and as a citizen of the cosmopolitan civil society of the world order,” the professor added.

Part of the work of the Constitutional Court has been focused on this aspect, examining the necessary conditions for amnesty and pardon processes, guaranteeing the rights of victims, the protection of minors and the conduct of forced recruitment, as well as the political participation of ex-combatants and the feasibility of the provisions for the end of the armed conflict.

###### Transitional justice issues

Regarding responsibility for war crimes, as provided by international criminal protocols, lawyer Ulfrid Neumann, professor at the Johann Wolfgang Goethe University of Frankfurt (Germany), argued that in the responsibility for command of superiors, the damages caused by civilian governments are of interest, all this from the principles of criminal law.

“Command responsibility is different from harm to a group of people, since it is a specific structure that causes that harm. These structural elements of superior responsibility occur where there is a hierarchical organization with actions that are attributed to the superior, and the subordinate takes action in response to an order,” the jurist explained.

Truth is essential when discussing responsibility, and that is why the seminar highlighted the value of having a commission in Colombia's transitional justice model to clarify the truth, as this has special importance for the victims.

“Se indicó que la verdad puede ser alcanzada a través de los procesos penales contra perpetradores. Es una condición necesaria, de procesos mínimos de reconciliación nacional, es un derecho de las comunidades vulneradas por los abusos masivos, como garantía de reconstrucción de su memoria colectiva y su identidad”, dijo el magistrado José Fernando Reyes.

metadata.og:description: Blindar los acuerdos y ofrecer la seguridad jurídica que requiere el proceso de paz. Esa, según el magistrado José Fernando Reyes Cuartas, ha sido la visión de la Corte Constitucional de Colombia frente a la justicia transicional con la que el país pretende superar el conflicto armado con las Farc. El magistrado expuso el balance del trabajo de esa entidad jurídica nacional en relación con el acuerdo de paz ante expertos nacionales e internacionales convocados al seminario Justicia Transicional: el modelo colombiano, que culmina este viernes primero de junio en EAFIT.
